1:
Gill and Henry both note that the chapter division is disputed, Gill reporting that Junius and Tremellius make the first fifteen verses part of the preceding chapter and Henry that some translators join these verses to it as belonging to the same vision. Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition: having pointed out the difficulties of the call, the Lord now prepares the prophet for his office by inspiring him with the word he is to announce. Clarke insists the eating must have passed in vision, though the meaning is plain, that the word is to enter the soul and be digested.

Henry expands the command at length. To eat the roll is to admit the revelation into the understanding, take its meaning aright, admit it into the heart and be affected with it, imprint it on the mind and ruminate upon it, take it entire and make no difficulty of it, and indeed take pleasure in it as in meat, so that the soul is nourished and it becomes meat and drink and necessary food. From this he draws a rule, that preachers should so take in the word in their studies that they are both well acquainted and much affected with the things of God, and can speak of them clearly and warmly together. Wesley works the figure grammatically, that the mouth is the proper instrument of eating but the belly is said to eat when the meat is digested, and takes the filling of the bowels for the fulness of the measure with which the word should be read and digested. Gill adds that the prophet did all he could toward eating but was not sufficient of himself, and was not to cast the roll out as soon as he had tasted it.

Calvin takes the eating for sincerity rather than study. A book was given him to eat because the servants of God ought to speak from the inmost affection of the heart; many have a tongue fluent enough but use it only for ostentation, and God makes their vanity a laughing stock because their labour is fruitless, the efficacy of the Spirit not being exerted unless the man called to teach applies his serious endeavours. He also presses the taste of the book: since it contained nothing but material for sorrow, the prophet either had put off all humanity or ought to have been grieved at finding himself the herald of vengeance. His answer is that the servants of God elsewhere show the opposite feeling, rough and stern like their work yet condoling with the miserable people, and that their grief did not hinder them; the prophet here pitied his people but acknowledged it could not be otherwise, and forgot the sorrow in the book because the justice of God prevailed and extinguished the too great humanity that might have delayed him. Calvin also guards the command: he is not told to eat everything, but forbidden to refuse the book whatever its taste, since its bitterness might have made him reject the threats.

The sweetness in the mouth is the last thing weighed. Wesley finds it sweet to receive things by revelation and to converse with God, and observes that the first part of ministerial work is usually pleasant. Ellicott says the same of the first impression made by a prophetic call, which must always be one of delight to those whose privilege it is to bear a message from God to their fellows, and notes that although this prophet does not add, as another seer does, that his belly was made bitter, the later account of his going in bitterness to a people indisposed to hear allows it to be inferred. Clarke draws the same comparison and gives it a moral: deep consideration of the awful matter in the word of God against sinners must afflict anyone who knows the worth of an immortal spirit.
4:
Calvin makes the order of the two acts the point. The volume is first given to the prophet and then transferred to the people, since he ought not to come empty and man of himself can bring forward nothing solid; and the rule holds for all the servants of God, that they should not heap up their own comments but pronounce what God teaches as if from his mouth, as Peter says that he who speaks in the church ought to speak the words of God. Gill puts the same sequence briefly, that he was qualified to prophesy only after he had eaten the roll.

The comparison with foreign nations is read as encouragement. Calvin reports the view that the prophet is animated to his duty because God demanded nothing too difficult, since a mission to nations whose speech he did not know would have laid on him a burden greater than he could bear. Clarke names the nations he was not sent to, neither the Chaldeans nor the Medes and Persians, and observes that even these would more likely have hearkened than his own countrymen. Gill takes the strange speech for a lip that is deep, difficult to be got at, and notes that although several prophecies in this book concern other nations, they all have relation to Israel and were chiefly on their account, so that he was never sent to deliver them abroad. Wesley reads the plural simply, of nations so many that he would have needed several tongues. Ellicott presses the reproach, that men far below them in privilege would gladly have yielded the heed they withheld, and answers the question it raises: only so could even a few be raised above the lowest spiritual plane, and the raising of those few leads at last to the elevation of many, while man, being accountable, must be left free to neglect the grace offered.

The clause that follows is a crux, and Calvin works through three renderings before giving his own. He reports that Jerome translates it as a supposition that God had sent him to them, though a negative particle stands in the way; that others, finding the phrase harsh, take the words for a form of swearing and render them affirmatively, which he says leaves the passage defective; and that others read it as saying that had he not been sent they would have heard him, since the people preferred vain prophecies to the truth and would embrace the fables of any impostor. This last he calls unsuitable here. His own preference is that but for the difference of speech God would rather have sent him elsewhere.

The refusal itself is traced past the prophet to God. Gill says the people were perfectly capable of understanding his speech, and that they did not hearken to him not because they rejected him and his words but because they rejected the Lord and his. Calvin presses it as consolation: teaching proudly rejected is a stumblingblock likely to break the spirits of the pious, and this reproach alone is often enough to recall the servants of God from their course, so the admonition is set in the midst that God himself is despised. Why take it ill to be valued as the God who is himself rejected is valued? Since the people are proud and unbelieving towards him, it is no wonder they do not reverently receive what a mortal man offers. Clarke prefers the marginal rendering, stiff of forehead and hard of heart, and remarks that the marginal readings here are very nervous and very correct. Both Ellicott and Wesley soften the word all, Wesley taking it for the far greater part though not every particular person and Ellicott for the people generally, as the word is often used in Scripture, since there were even then such saints among them as Jeremiah and Daniel.
8:
The hardening of the prophet answers the hardness of the people. Ellicott notes that the word rendered strong is the same rendered impudent of them, though it must carry a different shade in each case, and takes the thought from the figure of horned animals in their contests, God promising to make him the stronger. Gill is careful with the same point: the prophet is not to have the sort of impudence they had, but such a face, as the Hebrew has it, such spirit and courage that he should neither be ashamed of the words of the Lord nor afraid to speak them, so that they could not look him out of countenance. He adds that the Lord fits his ministers for the people he sends them to, all such boldness being a gift of his. Wesley draws a rule, that the more impudent men are in opposing religion, the more openly should the people of God appear in its defence.

Calvin explains why the obstinacy is named at all. God strengthens the prophet lest he despair at contending with such abandoned men, for what else was it than contending with stones, or striking a mountain? Yet Calvin turns it the other way too: had the prophet hoped for more fruit, that very ease might have made him negligent, since confidence makes us remiss when the work is not laborious. So the difficulty is set before him to rouse him, and the strength offered with it, that he might look for fortitude from another quarter and not spend his own in vain. Calvin then meets an objection: it may seem contradictory that a man given unconquered fortitude should still need exhortations, but God so tempers his favour that the faithful need excitements even while he supplies them with strength, breathing virtue into his exhortations.

The adamant is identified two ways. Gill derives the Greek name from its being unconquerable by hammer or fire, notes that it cuts iron and so is harder than stone, and reports that Bochart took it for the stone jewellers use to polish gems. Ellicott says simply that adamant is the diamond, and turns the comparison into a promise: the people were as hard as flint, but as the diamond cuts flint, so his words should be made by divine power to cut through their resistance. Calvin adds that though the whole world rise up against the servants of God his strength will be superior, as another prophet was told that they should fight against him and not prevail.

The last two verses narrow the commission. Calvin explains the repetition by the character of this prophet, who is more verbose than others because he accommodated his language to the speech then current among the exiles, a people not only rude and dull but obstinate, who had degenerated as much from the purity of their language as from that of their faith. On the order of receiving in the heart and hearing with the ears he holds the terms inverted, since we must perceive with the ear before we receive in the heart, and says those philosophize with more subtlety than truth who make the interior hearing come first, since the teaching does not penetrate the mind before the ear has received it. Ellicott makes the mission definite: it is limited for now to that part of the house of Israel already in captivity, a small part then though before his ministry ended it embraced the mass of them. He also marks the wording, that God sends him not to my people but to thy people, refusing to own them in their present state, while reminding the prophet that he is one of them and must guard against the same obduracy. Gill and Wesley both fix which captivity is meant, not the earlier deportation to the cities of the Medes but the one under Jeconiah.
12:
Whether the transport was bodily or visionary divides the voices sharply. Gill insists it was real and not visionary, as Kimchi thought, the Spirit lifting the prophet from the ground and carrying him in body to another company of captives along the same river, as Philip was caught away from the eunuch. Ellicott holds the opposite, that this too was done in vision, as in the later instances, one of which is expressly said to have been so. Clarke reports three explanations from Calmet, an impetuous wind, a momentary transport by the Holy Spirit, or such heavenly ardour that he ran off at once and seemed to fly; however it be understood, he says, the going to the captives was real. Calvin makes the point about agency rather than mode, that the agitation within the prophet availed nothing except through heavenly inspiration, and that he had to be carried beyond himself.

The voice and its source come next. Calvin calls it sonorous and unlike the usual voice of men, and Wesley hears an articulate sound of many angels with the rushing of the wheels behind it. Clarke assigns the blessing to the living creatures; Calvin traces it to both the creatures and the wheels, since a voice may fairly be ascribed to cherubim, while by the wheels God marks the motions that seem fortuitous and are yet governed. Ellicott leaves the source undefined, doubtless all that surround the throne, and adds that the Hebrew for wings touching one another is beautifully figurative, wings that kissed each one its sister; Calvin notes that some render the same word of wings striking or engaging in conflict, and holds that the kissing signifies conjunction. The place from which the glory is blessed is read three ways, Calvin taking it for the Temple, Wesley for a coming down from heaven and Clarke for the throne of glory.

Calvin gives the benediction a polemical edge. The people were querulous and murmured that they were treated more harshly than they deserved, and the glory of God is here set against their blasphemies; men who dare not utter gross reproaches curse his glory whenever they detract from his justice and accuse him of too much rigour. He adds that the creatures proclaimed him still reigning in his own Temple in the midst of that wretched slaughter, exercising his power especially as a judge. Henry adds that the mission made the angels rejoice and was meant to convince the prophet that his sender had power to bear him out, and that however sweet communion with God may be, his servant must serve his generation.

The bitterness of the going closes the passage. Clarke has him filled with indignation at the wickedness of his people and determined to speak without disguise, yet distressed at the heavy message he must deliver. Ellicott makes the contrast the point: the command was sweet and its performance bitter, but the hand of the Lord was strong upon him and he could not forbear, as another prophet in his discouragement had almost resolved to refuse and found the word a burning fire within, an experience every faithful teacher must more or less pass through. Wesley says the same, that the strong hand served not only to compel him to the work but to fit him for it. Calvin uses the phrase to mark off true prophecy from false: he does not mean the prophet was deprived of self-control, as profane men imagine of their own prophets, who were not of sound mind, for the prophets of God were of a sedate and composed mind; he means rather that visible marks were graven upon him, so that a man well known to his friends by appearance and character was separated from common life to represent something celestial, and so gained reverence for his teaching from a dull people to whom his message was distasteful.
15:
The place and its name are worked over. Gill reports Jarchi and Kimchi for its being a place name, gives the sense a heap of new fruit which the Vulgate follows, and cites Junius for a tract in Mesopotamia between two rivers, where he thinks the captives were settled both to keep them in and to make them defend a region left uninhabited by inundations. Wesley places it the same way, shut in by one river westward and another eastward. Clarke gives the same sense of a heap of corn, and the Syriac, he says, reads instead the hill of grief. Ellicott takes it for the mound of ears of grain, probably a place of especial fruitfulness, and grants it cannot be further identified, though it seems to have been the central place of the captivity.

What he did there is read three ways. Ellicott takes the seven days for mourning, noting that silence was the characteristic of mourners, sitting their proper attitude and seven days the set time, so that the prophet shows his sympathy with his people; he adds that the week answers to the week in which his fathers were consecrated to the priesthood, and that such a season of retirement was given to other great leaders, to Moses in his exile, to Elijah at Horeb, to Paul in Arabia and to our Lord in the wilderness. Clarke reads it as discipline: God perhaps kept him without revelation so long that the bitterness he had just confessed might be subdued and he might speak the words of God in the Spirit of God, and had he gone in a better spirit he would probably have been employed as soon as he reached the place. Calvin and Wesley make it simple waiting, Wesley having him mourn until the spirit of prophecy should open his mouth, and Calvin explaining that it was no negligence, since the office had been laid on him before any fixed commands were given, as an ambassador may be chosen before his instructions are.

Two smaller points are disputed. Ellicott finds the clause about sitting so difficult in the Hebrew that it has produced variant readings and a marginal correction, and proposes changing the vowel pointing so that it reads that he saw where they sat. Calvin dismisses as frivolous the view that makes the prophet a kind of monk who abhorred the wickedness of the people and sought solitude lest he contract a stain, holding that he had never removed from them at all but was drawn out of ordinary intercourse by the vision, and returned to his former life when it vanished. He takes the word rendered astonished to carry desolation, astonishment and wonder together, and thinks God prepared him so that his eventual speaking would surprise the people the more.

Whether the day was a sabbath is disputed too. Henry thinks it very probable that both this day and the day of the vision were sabbaths, which the house of Israel kept as well as they could in captivity, their conquerors not tying them to constant service as their Egyptian taskmasters had; lacking temple and synagogue they met by the river side where prayer was wont to be made, where their enemies had upbraided them with the songs of Zion. He adds that a man who had been musing on the things of God all the week was fit to speak in his name on the sabbath, and that this time he was not honoured with visions as before, since raptures are not the daily bread of the children of God. Gill allows that some think so but holds it neither certain nor necessary. Calvin uses the interval to show that God deals with his servants by degrees, first claiming them for his own, then showing them generally what work they have, and at last sending them out to perform it.
17:
The office is defined before its burden. Gill insists the watchman is meant in no civil sense but an ecclesiastical one, the Targum rendering the word teacher, and traces the office through the prophets of old to the ministers of the New Testament, holding it the same as that of bishops: it lies in watching over souls as shepherds over their flocks, that they go into right pastures and not astray, and as watchmen of cities, to give the time of night and notice of danger. To discharge it, he says, requires quick sight, diligence, sobriety, vigilance, courage and faithfulness; and it is sons of men who are put into it, not angels, sons of fallen Adam, weak and frail and mortal. Calvin reaches the same identification from the word itself, that bishop means watchman, and draws the consequence that pastors must acknowledge themselves set in stations from which they can be watchful. He presses two things: that this cannot be done unless they are endued with superior gifts and prevail in the grace of the Spirit above ordinary men, and that it is not enough for them to live as private men, since a lofty watchtower demands diligence and a power of observation.

Clarke divides the charge into three: the watchman must watch for the safety of the people, preach for their edification and pray for their eternal welfare. He adds a fourth condition, that the word must be received at the mouth of God, since God is jealous lest any words but his own be taught for divine doctrines and will have no more of human creeds than of traditions in the place of his word; no word can be successful in the salvation of sinners but that which comes from God. Every minister should be familiar with his Maker by faith and prayer, or what he preaches will be destitute of life, his hackneyed texts and sermons proving not bread from heaven but dry mouldy crusts.

The responsibility is then made personal and heavy. Calvin says the watchman must render an account of the diligence with which he goes through his watches, souls being committed to his care so that if they perish he must undergo punishment. But he guards against taking this as a transfer of authority: no mortal may condemn or absolve at his own discretion, and when God sends out his servants he does not resign that power, since the supreme authority remains with him and there is one lawgiver who can save and destroy. He recalls that this prophet elsewhere reproves the false prophets for keeping alive the souls that were dying and slaying the souls not devoted to death, and observes that proud men tyrannize over the conscience when they take the prophetic name and put themselves in the place of God.

Clarke turns the threat on the ministry of his own day. If the wicked man is not warned he dies in his iniquity, but his blood is required at the hand of the watchman. From this he addresses those who entered the ministry for a living and gather a congregation that they may feed on its fat, while souls die unconverted among them from day to day, never warned and never shown the way of salvation, probably because the man himself knows nothing of it; such take their tithes to the last grain and the last penny while those over whom they made themselves watchmen perish. He calls the boast of apostolical authority vain in men who do not the work of apostles, the boast of orthodoxy vain in men who neither show nor know the way of salvation, and pretensions to a divine call vain where no evangelist work is done. Gill states the death itself, not corporeal only but eternal, being the wages and issue of sin unless grace prevent.
19:
Calvin makes the first half of the charge a consolation. Though those meant to be brought back remain obstinate, the servants of God ought not to throw up their commission as useless, since by discharging it they free their own souls; if they are dumb dogs the destruction of souls is imputed to them, but once they have done their duty it should suffice them to be absolved in his judgment. He compares the word of Christ that those who enter a house should salute it, and if the house prove unworthy the blessing returns to themselves; so with prophets whose labour on wandering sheep proves unprofitable. On the wording he distinguishes impiety, the inward wickedness of the heart, from the impious way, the outward life comprehending all actions. Gill puts the duty plainly, to lay his evil before him and warn him to flee from wrath to come.

The turning of a righteous man opens the sharpest division here. Gill denies that it can mean one truly righteous or justified by the righteousness of Christ, since that righteousness is everlasting and no man can be turned out of it; the man meant is one denominated righteous from a righteousness of his own, outwardly reformed, consisting of a little negative holiness and a few moral performances, and from that a man may indeed apostatize. Clarke takes the words at face value and against exactly that reading: they plainly state that a righteous man may turn, commit iniquity and die in his sin, from which we see that he may fall from grace and perish everlastingly. To say the self-righteous are meant he calls absurd, since self-righteousness is itself a fall and the sooner a man falls from it the better; real righteousness of heart and life is what is meant. Calvin states the difficulty without resolving it here, asking how the just can turn aside when there is no righteousness apart from the spirit of regeneration, the seed of the Spirit being incorruptible and his grace never utterly extinguished, the Spirit himself the seal of an adoption that is without repentance.

Ellicott sets that question aside. Independently of any theological question, he says, Scripture here as often elsewhere represents the upright man as exposed to temptation and in danger of falling, so that the prophet must not only turn the wicked from his way but warn the righteous against the same; both terms are comparative, though they show a considerable difference of character already among the captives. Calvin puts the same duty as the second half of a twofold office, that pastors collect the dispersed sheep and retain those already gathered, since men are scattered by their own infirmity unless strengthened, so that pastors are guilty if the righteous fall away through their negligence. Gill widens the warning, that the righteous are to be told not to trust their own righteousness but to depend on the righteousness of Christ.

The stumbling-block is read two ways. Clarke and Wesley make it permission rather than act, Clarke saying that God permits the man to be tried and to fall in the trial, being repeatedly represented as doing what he only permits. Ellicott takes the word more broadly, as anything at which people stumble whether intended so or designed for their highest good, noting that Christ is foretold as a stumbling-block to both houses of Israel; he observes that this prophet uses the word oftener than all other writers of the Old Testament together, once of the riches of the people and once of the sinful Levites, and concludes that the meaning is a man perverting the gifts of God into an occasion of sin. Clarke closes with a saying from Gregory, that the pastor kills this man by being silent; Wesley adds that the apostate is the worst of men, because he falls from known ways of goodness.
22:
Henry is struck by the anticlimax. After so magnificent a discovery of God and so full a commission, we should have expected the prophet to be preaching at once to a great congregation, but his work at first seems not proportionable to the pomp of his call; he is retired for further learning instead. Henry reads that retirement as accommodation: by his unwillingness to go it would seem he was not thoroughly convinced that the God who sent him could bear him out, and so God favours him with another sight of his glory to animate him. He admires the condescension of it, that God should converse so familiarly with a son of man, a poor captive who had gone in bitterness of spirit and out of humour with his work; and he draws from it the benefit of solitude, how much it befriends contemplation, and how comfortable it is to be alone with God. Clarke makes the same point practically, that the plain was remote from observation and noise, so that the glory of God had room to manifest itself and its movements could be seen distinctly; Ellicott adds that the week of silence being past and the charge given, the constraining power of God sends him out to the final act of preparation.

What the hand of the Lord is gets two answers. Gill reports the Targum interpreting it of the spirit of prophecy remaining upon him, but prefers a fresh impulse of the Spirit stirring him up to attention. Calvin flatly rejects the first, calling the exposition that makes the hand of God the prophetic office cold, and takes it for power, the agitation of the Spirit, so that the prophet felt himself carried forward neither by human strength nor by any impulse of his own.

Calvin also meets the objection that God is trifling with his servant. It looks like a change of plan when the duty of teaching is imposed, the man sent abroad, and then ordered to shut himself at home. His answer is that the authority of the prophet was confirmed by exactly this, since God governed his tongue for speech and for silence alike: he was made a teacher, yet restrained himself until God should suggest what to say, was ordered to be silent and obeyed, and only when God dictated the words did he begin. Had he spoken directly upon his appointment, levity might have been objected against him, but showing alacrity and yet keeping silence added weight to his teaching. Calvin adds that the prophet supposed himself led out to proclaim the commands of God at once, and was mistaken.

The vision and the command that follows it are read variously. Gill notes the obedience, that he went where ordered without knowing what he would hear. Calvin makes the falling and the raising a doctrine: the faithful cannot collect their minds at the sight of the glory of God unless he prop them up, and this prophet had to acknowledge himself dead when he felt the Spirit living in his mind, since as the soul gives life to a man so the Spirit of God is a supernatural life in him; profane men celebrate free will and our natural faculties because they have never tasted the other. Wesley turns the vision on the reader, that we are not now to expect such sights but have a favour nothing inferior if by faith we behold the glory of the Lord and are changed into the same image. On the shutting up, Clarke says only to hide for the present, since the reason is immediately given; Ellicott offers either a beginning of the prophecies in a private way, given the disposition of the people, or a further period of absolute silence and meditation before the work; and Wesley makes it a sign, foresignifying the shutting up of the people in Jerusalem.
25:
The bands are read literally by some and figuratively by others. Clarke takes them plainly, that his countrymen will rise and confine him to prevent his prophesying, and Wesley that he shall be straitly confined. Gill offers three possibilities without choosing: that the Jews, taking him for a madman by his gestures, would bind him and keep him indoors; or that the bands are the obstinacy of the people; or that they are the divine order itself, restraining him for the present. Ellicott argues firmly for the figurative sense. His contemporary was indeed thrown into prison and even into a dungeon, but there is no trace of such treatment in this book, nor is it likely among the captives of Nebuchadnezzar or possible under the administration of Daniel; and a similar laying on of bands later, though for another purpose, must be figurative. The compulsion, he concludes, was moral: his countrymen should so refuse to hear him that declaring his prophecies would become practically impossible, and he would be as if bound.

Calvin allows both readings and declines to decide. The metaphorical sense is not unsuitable, the perverseness of the people binding the prophet as if with ropes; and he supports it from Paul, who told the Corinthians that his mouth was open toward them and his heart enlarged, while their own bowels were straitened. Since men by their depravity hinder the course of doctrine, the malice of the unteachable may fairly be called ropes binding faithful teachers. Yet if anyone prefers the literal sense, that too is appropriate: the people were not yet prepared for instruction, and had the prophet spoken at once they would have laid hands on him.

The dumbness is then transferred to God. Clarke reads it as withheld matter, God giving him no message because they are so rebellious that further warning is useless. Ellicott notes the shift of figure, that the silence is attributed not to the rebellious house, who brought it about, but to God, whose providence was its ultimate cause, and takes it as a strong way of expressing the difficulties of the ministry. Calvin reconciles the two, since the people rejected prophecy through their own intemperance and God deprived them of the benefit as unworthy; and he presses the consequence, that the ceasing of all prophecy is a sign of divine vengeance, for as God shines on us by his instruction and gives in it a pledge of his favour, so when instruction is removed it is as if he hid his face. God does not desist at the first wearying, he adds, but rises early and keeps watch while it is yet night, and only at length takes his teaching away; whence the Church counts destitution of prophets among the extreme signs of anger.

The reopening of the mouth closes the chapter. Gill allows either that God will speak when he has given all the instructions, or that he will speak again with fresh orders. Ellicott looks forward to the later verses where, after the destruction of the city, the mouth of the prophet is shut no longer; until then, though greatly restrained in ordinary utterance by the opposition of the people, there would be times when God gave him a message with such power that he was constrained to declare it, and such are the messages this book now begins to record. Calvin finds the manner remarkable: ambassadors are usually told to try what courteous discourse can do, but God has his prophet begin with an insult, so that the people may understand he is not sent because there is hope of their growing wise, but that he may strike and wound them further. Clarke states the alternative without heat: he who finds obedience to the voice of God his interest should be steadfast, and he who disregards the warning may go his own way and abide the consequences.
